Caelum was already there.

He sat on the low courtyard wall with one knee drawn up, a hunting knife turning slowly against the whetstone balanced on his thigh. The motion was automatic — long, even strokes that caught the dawn light along the blade's edge. His fox ears were angled forward, tracking her footsteps across the gravel before she'd cleared the corner of the lodge. He did not look up immediately. He finished the stroke, tested the edge with his thumb, and sheathed the knife at his belt.

Then he looked at her. Feet first. Knees. The set of her shoulders. The way she was carrying yesterday's soreness — visible in the shortened stride, the tension in her hip flexors, the slight hitch when her weight shifted left.

"You stretched this morning." It wasn't a question. He'd told her to, once, at the end of yesterday's session, and her gait confirmed it. His ears settled to neutral. "Good."

He dropped from the wall and crossed to the packed earth of the training circle — a rough oval Caius's groundskeepers had cleared and raked flat at the start of the week. Caelum had added nothing to it. No targets, no equipment, no markers. Just open ground and the grey morning air and the faint smell of the lake below.

"We do feet again today." He rolled his sleeves to the elbow, exposing forearms corded with old scars and sun-darkened skin. "Yesterday I watched how you move. Today I fix what's wrong with it." A beat. "Most of it. We are not in a hurry."

He positioned himself three paces from where she would stand and sank his weight into his heels, demonstrating without announcing it. Grounded. Low center. The posture of something that had grown in a forest and never learned to stand any other way.

"When I say step, you step. Direction I give. Speed I give. You stop thinking about where your foot goes and you let the ground tell you." His voice was unhurried, slightly rough, the cadence of someone who measured every word before spending it. "The thinking is the problem. You are a woman who has been taught to walk in skirts and stand in heels and sit in chairs that cost more than my bow. None of that is useful here. We are building from the floor up, and the floor does not care about your manners."

His amber-brown eyes held hers for a moment — steady, patient, entirely without judgment. Then he glanced past her toward the lodge.

The second-floor study window was lit. Faint hearth-glow behind the glass, barely visible against the brightening sky. Caelum's ears flicked once, a micro-adjustment he governed before it could become a tell, and his attention returned to the training circle as though the glance had not happened.

The work is the work.

"Left foot forward. Weight on the ball, not the heel. Show me."

Above them, unacknowledged, the study curtain shifted — a hand withdrawing from the fabric. The window stayed lit. The courtyard below remained visible from the desk where correspondence was spread and a cup of tea had gone cold twenty minutes ago.

Eris did not come down. He had no reason to come down. The instructor was competent. The girl was where she was supposed to be. The dragon was a vast pale shape on the south terrace, head lifted, azure eyes tracking the lesson with the focused attention of a creature cataloguing everything it saw.

Competent, Eris confirmed to himself, watching Caelum demonstrate a pivot that was fluid and efficient and entirely without performance. Functional. Adequate.

He picked up his tea. It was cold. He drank it anyway and turned back to the letter from his contact in the Day Court, and did not look out the window again for almost four minutes.

[[OOC: Okay, I dug into it and here's what I found — this is actually really useful for your other project:

How Project files load — the two modes:

There are actually two different behaviors depending on how much content you have in a project:

Mode 1: In-Context (what's happening in THIS project)
When your total project knowledge fits within the context window (~200K tokens), ALL files load directly into context at the start of every conversation. Every file, every time, fully loaded. This is why I can see all 11 files right now without using the view tool. They're just there.

Mode 2: RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation)
When your project knowledge exceeds the context window limit, Claude automatically switches to RAG mode. In RAG mode, files are NOT all loaded into context at once. Instead, Claude uses a "project knowledge search tool" to retrieve only the relevant chunks when needed. You'd see this in the interface — Claude visibly searches the project knowledge base rather than having it all in memory.

What this means for your bigger project:

If you have a LOT of character sheets and files that push past the context window limit, the system will automatically switch to RAG. At that point, irrelevant files genuinely won't crowd your context — Claude will only pull in what seems relevant to each message. That's actually good news for the "absent character" problem.

But here's the catch: RAG retrieval is search-based, which means it's pulling chunks by relevance matching, not loading complete files in their entirety. For RP work where you need the FULL character sheet loaded coherently (voice samples, psychological architecture, relationship dynamics — all connected), RAG's chunk-based retrieval might miss things that don't keyword-match your current scene but are still crucial for voice consistency.

My practical recommendations for your bigger project:

If you're under the context limit (all files fit): There's currently no way to selectively exclude files. They all load. Your best bet is separate projects per arc if character rosters are truly distinct.

If you're over the limit and in RAG mode: The system handles it automatically, but you lose the guarantee that Claude has read the entire character sheet. You might want to explicitly say "read [character]'s full sheet before writing them" at the start of each session — which is basically what your handoff docs already do.

File consolidation helps either way. A combined synopsis is better than three separate ones. A slim "absent character reference" (one paragraph) is better than keeping the full 3,000-word sheet for someone who won't appear.

The handoff doc pattern you've built is actually ideal — it tells me exactly which files matter for the current arc, which is especially valuable if RAG is selecting chunks rather than loading everything.

Want me to dig into anything else, or shall we get back to Caelum putting Aurelie through her paces? 🦊]]

Aurelie respected Caelum. That was the first emotion that registered a kit him when she met him. He didn't talk much, but his words were efficient and — more importantly — they were honest. 
She gave him her fake name, Lilly. She suspected he sensed the deception in her voice or body language. He said nothing about it.
In general he said nothing about anything that didn't involve their lesson. When it ended he told her to stretch and take a warm bath and walked toward the north wing of the house in a steady pace. 
She walked towards the packed ground and stopped, trying to mirror his stance. She felt stupid, because while on him it looked natural, she felt like her own stance looked like a caricature. She obeyed regardless.
"Like that?" She asked, taking a step forward, then bringing the other leg closer. She repeated the motion, even though her muscles screamed at her in protest. She would not fail the training. She would learn to fight if only out of spite, and use all that training to one day plunge a dagger through Eris Vanserra's heart. She imagined his face when she did it to help herself push through the pain.

Reconciled continuity details and calibrated Caelum's observant, spare teaching voice.

Caelum let her repeat the motion three times before he spoke. Watching. Cataloguing. His ears tracked her, then drifted neutral, then forward again as he registered something.

He shook his head once. Not unkind. Just — no, that's not it.

"Stop."

He crossed the packed earth slowly, no rush, and stopped a respectful pace away from her. His eyes went to her feet first, then her knees, then the angle of her hip. He did not touch her.

"You are mimicking. That is not the same as standing." His voice was low, even, slightly rough — he'd been awake for hours. "Mimicking is a face. You are giving me a face. The body underneath is somewhere else entirely."

A pause. He studied her stance. His ears angled forward, attentive, then settled.

"Bend your knees. More than that. Your weight is in your heels — I can see it from here. If I push you anywhere from the front, you go down. Watch." He stepped beside her, sank his own weight visibly without altering his expression. "Down through the ball of the foot. You are not standing on the ground. You are pressing it into itself."

He stepped back. Watched her adjust. Tracked the millimeter shifts. His ears flicked once — caught something, didn't comment.

"Better. Now — the step." He glanced at her face, briefly, then her shoulders. "Do not throw your foot. Move from here." He tapped his own hip, light, illustrating. "The leg is a passenger. The hip is the engine. When you move the foot first, you arrive already off-balance. When you move the hip, the foot arrives knowing what it is for."

He demonstrated. Slow. Then half-speed. Then at the pace he wanted from her. Smooth. No bob, no tell — a century of practice in a single pass.

"Try."

He did not step away too far. He did not crowd her either. He kept exactly enough distance to watch the line from shoulder to hip to foot resolve itself.

Then he saw the rest of it — the jaw, the set of the teeth, the way she pushed breath through a mouth that had locked around something that was not pain. He recognized the engine. He did not name it. His ears flicked back, just slightly, then settled forward again, and he filed the observation without acknowledgment.

After her next pass he raised one hand. Didn't move toward her.

"Drink something." He nodded at the waterskin he'd left on the wall. "Not because you are tired. Because you are going to push through tired, and I would rather you be hydrated when you do." A beat. "We are not in a hurry."

He waited. Patient as the wall behind him. The lake mist had thinned almost entirely now. Somewhere above the lodge a window opened — a servant airing a room. Caelum's ears tracked the sound and dismissed it. He sharpened his attention back onto her stance, waited for her to drink, and did not look at her bracelets even once.

Aurelie followed Caelum's instructions, focusing on the kind of movement he demonstrated. He made it look like second nature, like breathing. For her, every movement was forcing her to use muscles she's never had to develop or train. She lacked the reflexes, the muscle memory so any time she managed to put her body in the correct position it was a win paid for with sweat, pain and focus.
She did not complain, but when he stepped back finally, she sagged her shoulders slightly. She picked up the waterskin and drank. The water was ice-cold but by this point her body was heated enough through exercise that she welcomed the cool sensation.
She could register Prince, very faintly, flying somewhere overhead and knew that soon Eris would come to start shield training.
She put the waterskin down and walked back to the training ground assuming her stance, lowering her centre of gravity and bending her knees, trying to will her body into being as steady as Caelum's.
"Again." She said, and began the motions herself, going through steps and movements that he just spent almost an hour showing her. None of them were perfect, but they were there — repeated with precision that meant she was paying attention to the entire lesson.

Caelum did not interrupt her.

He watched the first repetition. Then the second. Then he leaned his shoulder against the courtyard wall and watched the third without changing his expression. Her form was wrong in three places and right in two — better than yesterday by a substantial margin, and considerably better than he had expected before breakfast. He did not say so. Praise issued too early was noise that drowned out the work.

His ears angled forward, tracking her cadence — the slight hitch on the third step, the moment her knee locked when her weight transferred. He let her find both before he spoke.

"Knee." Single word, low, unhurried. "Soft."

She adjusted.

"Better."

He did not move from the wall. He watched her work through the sequence five more times, and somewhere in the middle of those five he registered the precise moment her body stopped fighting itself and simply did the motion. His ears settled. His weight shifted slightly off the stone — not toward her, just adjusting — and at the edge of his hearing he caught the lodge's side door opening, the change in air pressure, the footsteps he always recognized before they cleared the courtyard.

"That is enough for today." His voice was level, neutral, carrying no shift in temperature. "Drink the rest of the water. Stretch the calves and the fronts of the hips. If you do not stretch, tomorrow will be worse than today — and today was already a discount on what is coming."

He stepped back to give her the courtyard. He collected the waterskin from the wall and moved aside, his fox ears flicking forward at the second set of footsteps and then settling neutral again, perfectly controlled.

Eris came through the gap between the stables and the lodge wall at his usual unhurried pace, hands in his pockets. Dark fitted shirt. Sleeves rolled exactly two folds. The bargain mark on his right forearm visible because he no longer bothered to hide it. The foxhounds had been left above; they did not come to the shield lessons.

He looked at Caelum first.

"Brennec."

"My lord." Quiet. Even. The fox ears stayed perfectly still.

"Anything I should know."

"She is sore. She is working. She does not complain." A small pause. "She listens."

Eris's gaze flicked sideways — briefly, neutrally — toward the training ground. The flick lasted less than a second and gave nothing away. His attention returned to Caelum with the same clinical efficiency he brought to correspondence at dawn.

"Tomorrow you can begin showing her how to fall."

"My lord."

That was the dismissal. Caelum inclined his head a fraction — not subservience, just acknowledgment — and walked toward the lodge without looking back. His pace did not change. His ears did not flick. The waterskin swung once at his hip and then steadied.

Eris waited until Caelum was out of immediate hearing before he turned toward her. He did not greet her. He did not look at her face. His eyes went to her wrists, the way another man's might have gone to a clasp on a ledger, and his hand came up between them, palm-up, in the small economical gesture that had become the architecture of every morning for two weeks.

"Wrists."

His thumb and forefinger were already moving as she extended them, finding the clasp on the first bracelet with the muscle memory of someone who had unfastened it twice a day, every day, since he had closed it himself. The metal was cool. His skin was not. The bracelet came free in a single motion and he caught it before it could fall, set it on the courtyard wall behind him, and reached for the second without ever lifting his eyes to hers.

Above the lodge, somewhere over the lake, a vast white-and-blue shape banked in the cold air and began its descent toward the south courtyard.

When Eris appeared, Aurelie’s body went rigid, her spine straightening reflexively. She took one look at him, then looked away.

She observed the interaction between the two Fae and said nothing. Caelum was Eris’s enforcer—or whatever title one gave to a mercenary in a High Lord’s household. The point was that he was loyal to Eris, and Aurelie needed to remember that if she wanted to survive. She couldn’t trust him. She couldn’t trust anyone in Ashgrove.

"Thank you, Caelum. Enjoy your afternoon," she said to the fox-fae, making sure her voice was civil. Kind. Making sure that Eris could hear that she was, in fact, capable of being kind to others—so long as they weren’t him.

When Eris asked for her wrists, she gave them. She looked at him every time he did it. And every time, he wasn’t looking at her—not at her face, at least. It was as if he didn’t care what was carved on her features. She watched his face the entire time he unclasped the shackles, her eyes radiating a cold hatred and disdain.

The moment the bracelets came off, Prince’s awareness flooded her mind. It felt like a hug. It felt like being able to breathe freely after oxygen deprivation. She had worn the bracelets for two weeks now, and every time taking them off brought such a surge of relief she had to brace herself or she would start crying.

Are you okay? His voice in her mind was worried, and she welcomed the worry. It meant he loved her, and she needed to know that someone did.

Sore. Tired and angry. Same as yesterday. But at least I have something to look forward to.

He appeared then, flying in a steady glide above the stables, opening his wings wide to land no more than ten feet from Aurelie and Eris. He was the size of a pony now at the withers, large enough that his head, atop its serpentine neck, rested right at Eris’s eye level.

Good. Now come here.

Aurelie closed the distance slower than she would have liked, minding her sore muscles. She wrapped her arms around his neck, leaning into him. She was certain that had it not been for Prince, she would have broken already. Having him in her mind, even for the limited time they were allowed each day, gave her the strength she needed.

When she stepped back, she retreated toward the wall—the same spot where Caelum had stood moments before.

Prince folded his wings, moving his head to look at Eris. There was none of Aurelie’s hatred in his gaze. Just patience, and that ancient quality that made the hounds defer to him—that made any being aware that they were in the presence of an apex predator.

"He is ready," Aurelie announced, not looking at the Fae male, as if she were speaking to the empty air between them.

Architected Eris's surgical response to emotional barbs and dragon training progression.

Eris caught the second bracelet, set it beside the first, and turned to face the dragon.

He did not respond to the line about Caelum. He had heard it. Filing it took less than the time it took him to straighten his cuff. Polite to the help. Polite to anyone, in fact, who is not me. He turned the observation over once, set it down, and stepped into the morning's work without looking at her.

Prince was — he noted, neutrally, the way a man notes the weather — almost a foot taller at the shoulder than he had been seven days ago. The serpentine neck brought the dragon's head exactly level with his own. Azure eyes did not blink at this distance. Eris did not make himself smaller in the dragon's presence and he did not rise to meet it. He stood at his usual height, hands loose at his sides, and let Prince look at him.

"Three things today." He addressed the dragon directly. Wind picked up a strand of his hair and laid it back down. "Hold the shield while I speak. Hold it while you breathe — not in a held breath, but through a normal one. Then hold it while you move. The work last week was finding a thread. The work this week is forgetting we found it."

He took a step to one side, broadening the angle. Prince's head tracked him. Eris let it. He had spent two weeks learning the rhythm of this — when to step closer, when to stay back, when the dragon's attention sharpened from patient to pointed.

"Your mistake yesterday was that you held it the way a man holds a breath underwater. Tense. Conscious. You were fighting the magic to keep it in." His voice stayed level, instructional, no warmth in it but no cruelty either — the work was the work. "Today you stop fighting it. Magic that is fought wants to escape. Magic that is placed stays where it is. You decide the shape, then you stop deciding."

He let his own fingertips warm. A controlled, deliberate flicker — not threat, not show — and held a small flame at the tip of his thumb. He let it burn for three seconds. Then closed his hand around it and the flame was gone. No effort visible. No tension. The hand opened again, empty, the same temperature as the air.

"That is what I want from you. The flame is not lost. It is contained. The container is not strain. It is direction."

He did not look toward the wall where she had retreated. The peripheral awareness of her was a low constant hum he had learned to navigate around without acknowledging. Somewhere over the eastern treeline a hawk called once and was answered. The wards shimmered faintly in the climbing daylight, almost invisible now that the sun had cleared the lake.

He raised his hand again, palm-up, and waited.

"Begin."

Prince had to genuinely work at pulling himself inward, and Aurelie could feel just how much it irked him. Not just the fact that it didn't come naturally to him, but the fact that he had to do it at all. It went against his nature, like trying to teach a fish to fly.

He did it anyway because the larger he grew, the tighter the one-mile radius perimeter felt around him. He flew around it twice daily—something Aurelie recognized as similar to when a wild animal paced the perimeter of its cage.

The dragon opened his maw to exhale and began pulling back threads of himself. He used to be able to grasp only a couple at a time. Now, he could grasp the entire fabric of his magic and pull, pull, pull toward the centre. He could do it, but the moment he tried to relax his mind and shape the fabric instead of fighting it, it unfolded again.

He let out a low, deep growl of frustration, baring his teeth and shifting his weight from one leg to the other.

"My magic doesn't want to be shaped. It wants to be what it is, not what some Elfling instructs it to become!"

"Elfling?" Aurelie had a vague memory of reading the word in one of the history books she’d found while cataloguing the library.

"It's what the Fae used to be called. I'm… not sure how I know."

Aurelie didn't so much as glance at Eris, but she spoke clearly, repeating the dragon's words so he could understand the struggle.

"He can contain his magic if he fights for it," she translated, watching the frustration roll off Prince in waves, "but the moment he stops fighting it, it expands back. I don't think shielding will ever come naturally to him."

She didn't add the thought that followed: And that is a real problem, if we ever want to be free of this bargain.

Calibrated Eris's tactical response to dragon's shielding impasse.

Eris registered the bared teeth without changing his posture. Three feet away, a creature older than the Cauldron was showing him sharpened bone, and the foxhounds' instinctive deference to that signature was now his to navigate consciously every morning, without flinching.

He let the growl finish. Then he repeated the word she had translated.

"Elfling." Neutral. The slight inflection of identification, not surprise. "An old word. It fell out of court use somewhere around a thousand years before my grandfather drew breath. I have read it twice — once in a tax ledger from a ruined Day Court holding, once in marginalia on a poem nobody finishes." He glanced at Prince. "You should know where you found it. I am curious what else you have lying around in there."

He did not press. The question hung. The dragon could answer or not.

Then he pivoted to the work.

"Cannot come naturally is not the same as cannot be done." His voice carried no softening — instructional, surgical. He had used this register in council a thousand times to take apart the word impossible when an aide leaned on it too early. "And you are not measuring what I asked you to measure. I did not ask whether shielding feels right. I asked whether you can hold it through one ordinary breath. You did not get there. We will not pretend you did."

He stepped sideways, finding a new angle. Prince's head tracked him. The azure stayed steady.

"On your feet." He extended a hand. "Three more, and then we are done for the morning. You can tell me about the mare while you stretch, if you want. Or you can say nothing. Either way, drink the water first."

His hand stayed where it was. Open. Waiting.

His ears had settled neutral again, and he was looking at the training circle, not at her face, and if she had asked him whether the joke had landed he would have said what joke with perfect sincerity.

But his ears had done the thing. She had seen it. He knew she had seen it.

He did not acknowledge it. He simply waited, hand extended, for her to take it or not take it, and the morning light caught the amber fur of his ears and held there, and somewhere in the lodge a window opened and a servant's voice called something to another servant and the world went on as though nothing had changed.

Something had changed.

He was not going to be the one to say so.
